blocks.text: This is also why a mesh jersey holds up well visually as it ages: there is no applied layer sitting across the holes to crack or lift, and the design fades with the fabric rather than separating from it.

text: Mesh is less abrasion-resistant than a solid knit of the same weight. Fewer fibers per unit area means less material between the floor and the wearer.

In basketball that matters less than it would in a sport with sliding, but it is not nothing — a player who takes a charge onto a wooden floor is putting their whole weight through a small area of open fabric.

It also snags. An open mesh will catch on a watch, a ring or a rough bench edge in a way a solid fabric will not, and a pulled thread on a mesh is more visible than on a knit. Neither is a reason to avoid it in this climate; both are reasons to keep a spare.
An open knit dries considerably faster than a solid one, which is the practical advantage that shows up between sessions rather than during them.

A mesh tank hung after a game is dry in a fraction of the time a denser jersey takes, and for a team playing two games in a tournament day that is the difference between a dry jersey and a damp one. It is a genuine reason to prefer mesh for tournament kit specifically.

The care rule that matters is the machine rather than the temperature: mesh should not go in with anything that has a hook, a zip or velcro on it. Those catch the open structure and pull threads in a way they cannot on a solid fabric, and a pulled thread on a mesh is immediately visible.

Beyond that it behaves like any dyed polyester — cold water, inside out, no fabric softener, and air drying rather than heat. The softener point matters more here than elsewhere, because it coats the fibers and closes some of the airflow the fabric was bought for.

sections.h3: When a solid knit is the better answer

text: Mesh is not automatically right, and there are three cases where it is not.

A light-colored game jersey where players layer underneath — the opacity problem outweighs the airflow benefit. A practice set that takes daily abuse — durability matters more than a marginal temperature difference in a garment nobody is looking at. And a set that will be reissued across four rosters, where the additional wear compounds.

For those, a denser knit with good moisture handling is the more sensible garment, and the temperature difference in an air-conditioned gym is smaller than the specification sheets suggest. Which of the two suits your program comes down to the same question every fabric decision does — what the gym is actually like in February rather than what the label claims.

items: Choose the mesh grade against the body color. Light colors want a finer mesh; dark ones can take an open one.
Ask who layers underneath, because that decides the opacity requirement more than the color does.
Scale the design to the fabric — bold shapes and large numbers on an open mesh, anything on a fine one.
Order a spare or two. Mesh snags, and a snag is more visible than wear.
Match the shorts fabric deliberately rather than by default, so the two halves of the set behave the same way in the wash.

basketball-practice-jerseys.h2: Worn Four Times More Often, Looked At Far Less
basketball-practice-jerseys.lede: A game jersey is worn twice a week in front of an audience. A practice jersey is worn four or five times a week in front of nobody, thrown in a bag damp, and washed in whatever is available. It is a different garment doing a different job, and specifying it as a cheaper version of the game set gets it wrong in both directions.

sections.h3: Where the money should go instead

text: On a game jersey, the budget goes into appearance and into the fabric behaving well for two hours at a time. On a practice jersey those are the wrong priorities.

What matters here is abrasion resistance, recovery after repeated washing, and color that stays separable across a squad. What does not matter is a design anyone will study, player names, or a premium hand feel.
The result is usually a cheaper garment than the game set, and one specified more carefully rather than less.

sections.h3: Two colors, and why it is the whole point

text: The single highest-value decision on a practice order is splitting the squad across two contrasting colors.

It means scrimmages divide instantly, without pinnies. Pinnies are the least popular piece of equipment in amateur basketball — they are shared, they are rarely washed, and players resent them. A two-color practice set removes them from the program entirely.
It costs nothing extra. The same order, the same setup, half the jerseys in each color. Programs that discover this usually wonder why they ever did it any other way.
The ratio that works for game jerseys does not transfer, because the frequency is not comparable.

One practice jersey per player means it is worn Monday, worn damp on Tuesday, and worn stiff on Wednesday. Two means there is always a dry one. Three means a program practicing five or six days a week is not doing laundry mid-week — which for a school with no laundry facility is the difference between the system working and not.
This is also the cheapest line on any uniform order, which makes under-ordering it a strange economy. A third practice jersey costs less than almost anything else on the sheet.

items: The neckline and armhole bindings. Repeated pulling on and off stretches them past recovery long before the fabric itself thins.
Ground-in floor dirt. Court sealant and rubber transfer onto light fabrics and set with heat, which is why a light practice set is unrecoverable by February.
Color separation. Two practice colors that fade at different rates stop being distinguishable, which defeats the reason they exist.
The hem. Tucked and untucked repeatedly, and the first place a cheaply finished garment fails.
Nothing about the design. On a dyed garment there is no applied layer to crack, which is one fewer failure mode than a screen-printed practice set has.

text: There is a second way to solve the scrimmage-split problem and it is worth pricing against the two-color approach.

A reversible practice jersey is one garment with a different color on each face. Every player owns one, sides are called by asking half the squad to turn theirs inside out, and the program buys fifteen garments instead of thirty.

The trade is that a reversible is a heavier, warmer garment — two layers of fabric bonded together — which in a Florida gym is a real cost rather than a technicality. It is also more expensive per unit, so the saving is smaller than the halved count suggests.

Which one suits a program comes down to the gym. A cool, well-conditioned hall makes reversibles the tidier answer; a warm one makes two thin sets the more comfortable one, and where reversibles are and are not worth it works through the arithmetic.
Whether practice jerseys need numbers depends entirely on how the coach runs a session.

A coach working with eighteen players calling instructions across a court wants numbers, and they save real time. A coach with twelve who knows every face does not, and skipping them lowers the cost noticeably across a full set.

Where numbers are used, they can be simpler than on a game jersey — front only, or a smaller size. Nobody is reading them from the bleachers, so the legibility rules that govern a number seen from the back row do not apply with the same force.

blocks.text: What practice jerseys should not have is player names. They add cost to a garment that will be replaced long before the roster is, and they stop it being handed to next year's squad.

sections.h3: What it saves the game set

text: The strongest argument for practice gear is not about practice at all. It is about what happens to the game jerseys without it.

A game set absorbing four days a week of drill work is worn out in one season rather than three. For a program that reissues kit across rosters, that difference is the whole economics of the uniform budget.

And it is bought back for a fraction of what a replacement game set costs. If a budget will not stretch to both a full game set and practice gear, the honest advice is to buy a simpler game set and keep the practice jerseys, rather than the other way round.

items: Count the squad and multiply by two, or three if you practise most days.
Split the count across two contrasting colors, half and half.
Choose the denser knit unless your gym is genuinely unbearable, in which case take the open one and order an extra per player.
Choose dark colors over light ones. Floor dirt is the thing that retires practice gear, and it shows on light fabric within weeks.
Order them with the game set on one job, so the setup is paid once and the colors match across everything.

text: One last thing worth deciding at order time: who owns them. A practice set issued to players and taken home is laundered fifteen different ways and comes back in fifteen conditions; one kept by the program and washed centrally lasts longer and costs somebody an evening a week. Neither is wrong, and the answer changes how many spares are sensible.

basketball-practice-shorts.h2: The Item Most Likely to Leave in Somebody Else's Bag
basketball-practice-shorts.lede: Practice shorts are the cheapest thing on a uniform order and the most frequently lost. They come off in a gym, go into a shared bag, and reappear on a different roster three weeks later. Any specification that ignores that is solving the wrong problem — durability matters, but replaceability matters more.

sections.h3: Order more than you think you need

text: A practice jersey usually comes home. A pair of practice shorts frequently does not, and the difference is that shorts are removed in the gym while a jersey is worn out of it.
Across a season, a squad of fifteen will typically lose three or four pairs. That is not carelessness; it is what happens when identical black shorts are in twelve bags on the same bench.
So order two per player and two or three spares, rather than one per player and hoping. The spares cost less than the mid-season reorder they replace, and they arrive matching.

sections.h3: Pockets, and why practice is different

text: Most leagues do not permit pockets on game shorts, and there is a sound argument against them in play — a pocket is somewhere a finger catches during contact.
None of that applies to practice. Nobody is being fouled hard in a shooting drill, and a pocket is genuinely useful for a phone, a key or a mouthguard between sessions.
It is one of the few places where practice kit can reasonably be better specified than game kit rather than worse, and it costs very little. Ask the players; they will have a view.

sections.h3: Inseam on a garment nobody photographs

text: Inseam is a style decision on a game short and a comfort decision on a practice pair.

Longer shorts are cooler in the sense that they do not ride, and warmer in the sense that they cover more leg. Shorter ones move more freely and are what most players choose when asked. On a garment worn five times a week the players' preference should carry more weight than the program's look.

The measurement still needs to be proportional across the size run rather than fixed — the same inseam sits at completely different points on a five-foot-two guard and a six-foot-six center, and a set cut to one number fits badly at both ends.

sections.h3: What fails, and in what order

items: The waistband elastic. Loses recovery after enough cycles, and it is the failure that retires a pair rather than making it look worn.
The drawcord. Frays where it exits the eyelet. Flat cord outlasts round cord by a considerable margin.
The seat. Floor abrasion from sitting, sliding and taking charges, and the one place a lighter fabric shows through first.
The hem. Caught underfoot, stood on, and pulled. A double-needle hem is worth the fractional cost on a practice pair.
Color, on light shades. Court dirt on light grey practice shorts is permanent within a season.

sections.h3: Why practice shorts outlive practice jerseys

text: This surprises programs ordering their first full practice set, and it changes how many of each to buy.

A practice jersey is pulled on and off constantly, which stretches its neckline and armholes, and it absorbs most of the sweat. A pair of shorts is put on once at the start of a session and taken off at the end, and it takes far less handling.

The result is that shorts usually outlast jerseys by a season or more in wear terms — while being lost far more often. So the ratio to buy is not one to one: more jerseys per player because they wear out, and more spare shorts because they disappear.
For a squad of fifteen, three jerseys and two pairs of shorts per player, plus three spare pairs, is the arrangement most programs settle on after a season of finding out.

sections.h3: Matching them to the rest of the kit

text: Practice shorts do not have to match the game set and there is a reasonable argument that they should not.

A separate practice color makes it obvious at a glance which set a player has grabbed, which matters on a game day when the wrong shorts are in the bag. It also stops a program's game shorts being quietly absorbed into practice use, which is the most common way a game set is destroyed early.
Where they do match, order them on the same job. Two orders placed months apart produce two versions of the same color, and on a set where the jersey and shorts are worn together that is visible.

blocks.text: A useful arrangement several programs use: game shorts in the team color, practice shorts in plain black or charcoal regardless of the team's palette. Cheaper, harder to lose track of, and it keeps the game pair for games.

text: Players routinely take one size in a jersey and a different size in shorts, and ordering both from a single letter is where most shorts exchanges come from.
Waist is the measurement that decides it. It takes fifteen seconds per player and it is not the number anyone volunteers, so it has to be asked for specifically.
It is also worth asking about fit preference. Some players want shorts sitting at the waist and some on the hip, and the difference between those two is a full size on the same person.

items: Two per player, plus two or three spares. This is the item that goes missing.
Take waist measurements separately from the jersey sizing rather than inferring them.
Decide on pockets. Practice is the one context where they earn their place.
Choose a dark color, and consider a different one from the game shorts so the two sets stay separate.
Order with the rest of the kit so the setup is paid once, even if the color is deliberately different.

text: And label them. A set of identical black shorts in a shared locker room is the definition of an item that goes missing, and a number inside the waistband — small, printed, not visible when worn — cuts the losses substantially for no cost at all.

basketball-warm-up-jerseys.h2: Twenty Minutes on Court Before Anybody Tips Off
basketball-warm-up-jerseys.lede: A warm-up jersey is worn in front of the same crowd as the game jersey, for a fifth of the time, doing a completely different job. It has to come off quickly, it has to keep a player warm while they are not yet warm, and it has to look like the program. Most teams treat it as a spare shirt. It is the piece of kit most seen and least specified.

text: A gym before a game is the coldest it will be all evening. The air conditioning has been running, the crowd is thin, and the players have been sitting on a bus.

The warm-up's job is to hold heat in during that period and then to be gone within about fifteen seconds when the starters are called. Everything about the specification follows from those two requirements.
It is also, in practice, the garment a crowd looks at longest without a ball in play. That is worth designing for, and most programs do not.

sections.h3: Getting it off in fifteen seconds

items: A full-length zip or snaps come off fastest and can be removed over a jersey without disturbing it. The most practical choice and the most common at higher levels.
A quarter-zip is a compromise: warmer at the neck, slower to remove, and it has to go over the head.
A plain pullover shooting shirt is the simplest and the slowest, and it will pull the game jersey with it if the fit is close.
Sleeveless shooting shirts remove quickly and provide almost no warmth, which suits a warm gym and defeats the purpose in a cold one.
Snap-away sides on full warm-up pants are the equivalent decision for the lower half, and they matter more, because pants over shoes are otherwise slow.

text: A warm-up garment has to be warmer than the jersey underneath it and light enough that a player is not overheating by the end of the shoot-around.
In Florida that balance sits lighter than most catalogues assume. A brushed-back knit is usually enough; a fleece-lined warm-up is a garment for a January gym in Ohio and an oven in one in Orlando.

The sleeve is where the warmth matters most, because the shoulders and upper arms cool fastest while a player is standing. A lighter body panel with a warmer sleeve is the arrangement that works in this climate and it is worth specifying rather than accepting a uniform weight throughout.
The game jersey is constrained. Numbers have to be a certain size, contrast has to work at distance, and association rules limit what can go where.

A warm-up has almost none of those constraints. It can carry the program name at full width, a crest at a size the jersey cannot accommodate, a sponsor, a season, or a design that would be illegible on a playing garment.

It is also worn off the court — travelling, in corridors, at tournaments — which makes it the highest-visibility item a program owns. Designing it as a variation on the game jersey wastes that, and putting the program's name across the chest is usually a better use of the space than a number.

blocks.text: If a warm-up will be worn during play as a layer rather than only before it, the association rules do apply and are stricter — usually a single solid color matching the jersey. Check the wording before designing something that cannot be worn when it is needed.

sections.h3: How many, and who gets one

text: Every player who takes the floor, plus the bench, which in practice means the whole roster.

A partial set is the arrangement that looks worst — a warm-up line where five players are in team kit and seven are in whatever they own reads as a program that ran out of money, which may be true and does not need advertising.
Because it is worn briefly and not under contact, a warm-up needs fewer spares than a jersey does. One or two across a squad covers the losses, and the garment itself will outlast two game sets.

sections.h3: Where it sits in the budget

text: For most programs this is the third purchase, after game kit and practice gear, and there is a reasonable argument it should be the second.

The case for it is visibility per dollar. A warm-up is seen by the crowd for twenty minutes a game and by everybody else on travel days, and it lasts longer than either of the other two sets because it takes no contact.

The case against is that it does not affect play. A program choosing between practice gear and warm-ups should take the practice gear, because that protects the game set — but the warm-up is the next thing to buy, and what practice kit is actually protecting explains why that order matters.

items: Decide the removal mechanism first — full zip, quarter zip, or pullover. It is the functional decision and everything else is styling.
Specify the weight against a Florida gym rather than a catalogue default. Lighter than you would think, with the warmth in the sleeves.
Design it as its own garment, not as the game jersey with sleeves. This is the item people look at longest.
Order one for every player on the roster, including the bench, plus one or two spares.
Check the association rules if it might be worn during play as well as before it.

basketball-training-jerseys.h2: Between the Game Set and the Practice Set
basketball-training-jerseys.lede: A training jersey sits in the gap most programs discover in their second season: the game set is too good to wear at a Tuesday session, and the practice set is too rough for a scrimmage against another school. It is the garment for everything in between — camps, clinics, tryouts, open gyms, and the sessions where the program is being looked at.

text: A joint session with another program, where practice gear looks unserious and the game set is at risk.
A camp or clinic run by the program, where participants are not on the roster and the kit is doing marketing as much as identification.
Tryouts, where a numbered garment that can be collected and reused across years is worth far more than a named one.
And summer play, where a team is representing the program without being in its formal competition kit.

sections.h3: What makes it different from practice gear

text: Practice gear is specified for abuse and nothing else. A training jersey has to survive abuse and still look like a garment somebody chose.

In practice that means the program mark rather than a bare number, a color that belongs to the identity rather than whatever was cheapest, and a finish that holds its shape after being handled by fifty camp participants.
It also means it is a garment the program can hand to somebody who is not on the roster — a visiting player, a camp attendee, a prospective recruit — without it looking like a hand-me-down.

items: Numbers, never names. A training jersey has to fit whoever picks it up next year, and a name ends that immediately.
Sequential rather than roster numbers. Numbering a set one to twenty rather than by this year's squad makes it reusable and makes a missing garment obvious.
Front and back. At a camp or tryout, coaches are identifying players from both sides and often from a scorer's table.
Larger than a practice number, smaller than a game one. Read from courtside rather than from the bleachers.
A program mark, not a season. Anything that dates the garment shortens its life for no benefit.

sections.h3: Sizing a set that is not for a specific roster

text: This is the one garment where ordering to a size distribution rather than to a roster is the right approach.

A training set has to fit next year's squad as well as this one, and a camp set has to fit whoever registers. That means a wider spread than a game set needs, weighted toward the middle sizes where most players sit.

For a squad of fifteen, a training set of twenty in a spread from small to double-extra-large will cover several years of rosters and most of a camp. It is a different purchase from a game set and should be counted differently.

blocks.text: Because it is not sized to a person, a training set is also the easiest kit to loan out — to a visiting team that arrives with a color clash, or to a player who has forgotten theirs. Programs that keep a numbered training set rarely need pinnies at all.

text: A summer camp is where a training set earns most of its value, and it is worth specifying with that in mind rather than adapting a set afterwards.

Camp participants are not on the roster, are frequently a wide range of ages, and take the jersey home at the end of the week in some programs and hand it back in others. Both models work; they need different quantities and different size spreads.

Where the jerseys are handed back, sequential numbering makes the count obvious at the end of each day and the set serves several summers. Where they are kept, the jersey is doing marketing all year in a way a game jersey never does, which is a reason to put the program's name on it rather than just a number.

Either way the sizing runs wider than a roster set — down into youth sizes if the camp takes younger players, and further up than a squad needs. It is the one order where over-ordering the ends of the range is sensible rather than wasteful.

sections.h3: Fabric for a garment worn by everybody

text: A training jersey is washed more times by more people than any other item a program owns, and frequently by whoever ran the camp rather than by a player.

That argues for a denser knit that holds color and shape through inconsistent laundering, and against anything delicate. It also argues for a mid-tone color rather than a light one, because light training kit collects marks from hands that are not being careful.

The airflow argument that governs a game jersey applies with less force here, because a training session is rarely as intense as a game and the garment is not being worn for two hours at a stretch. Where a gym is genuinely hot, what a Florida gym does to a fabric is still the reference, but the answer leans one step denser than it would for game kit.

sections.h3: Where it earns its place in the budget

text: A training set is not the first thing a program buys and it is frequently the item with the longest life.

Because it is numbered rather than named, unsized to a roster, and worn in lower-intensity settings, a well-specified training set can serve four or five years while a game set serves two or three. Per season it is among the cheapest kit a program owns.
It also removes a recurring cost. Programs without one buy pinnies, lose pinnies, and buy them again — and pinnies are the item players most dislike wearing.

items: Count for the roster plus a margin, not for the roster exactly. This set has to fit future squads too.
Number sequentially rather than by this year's roster, front and back.
Choose a mid-tone color from the program's palette that hides marks and holds through inconsistent washing.
Take the denser knit. This garment is laundered by more people, less carefully, than anything else you own.
Order it with the rest of the kit so the setup is paid once and the colors belong to the same family.
